background.source: The Catcher in the Rye by J.D. Salinger is a novel that delves into the complexities of being human, particularly through the eyes of the iconic teenage protagonist, Holden Caulfield. Originally published for adults, this novel has become a staple in the world of adolescent literature, famous for its themes of angst and alienation, as well as its critiques of societal superficiality. Through Holden's narration, the reader is taken on a journey of self-discovery, pondering issues of innocence, identity, belonging, and connection, while also discussing controversial topics such as sex and depression. With over 65 million books sold and a million copies sold each year, The Catcher in the Rye has gained global recognition and praise. The novel's social criticisms and discussions on human nature have made it an enduring classic and a must-read for those seeking insight into the complexities of being human.
background.target: The Great Gatsby is a classic novel by F. Scott Fitzgerald that is set in the Jazz Age on Long Island, near New York City. The story follows the first-person narrator Nick Carraway and his interactions with the mysterious millionaire Jay Gatsby, who is obsessed with reuniting with his former lover, Daisy Buchanan. The novel explores themes of social class, inherited versus self-made wealth, gender, race, and environmentalism, while also examining the concept of the American Dream through its cynical attitude. Despite receiving mixed reviews upon its release, The Great Gatsby has become a literary masterpiece and a part of American popular culture. However, it has also faced criticism for its alleged antisemitic stereotyping. Through its characters and their pursuit of happiness, the novel brings to light themes of moral nothingness and the dream catcher concept that allows individuals to chase a dream that is larger than life but may, in the end, leave one with nothing.
